boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Middle Boggy Depot record (February 13, 1864) in Operations in the Indian Territory [February 1864]. Phillips's expedition of February 1-29 (the Canadian River skirmishes of February 5-8, the march to near Fort Arbuckle and the return) is context; the live page's Red River Campaign label and March-April dates are not adopted. Campaign-wide marches, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Three companies of the 14th Kansas Cavalry Regiment and a section of Howitzers [US] and the Seminole Battalion, Company A, 1st Choctaw and Chickasaw Cavalry Regiment, and a detachment of 20th Texas Regiment [CS], with no numerical bounds; the live field is blank. Britton says Phillips left Fort Gibson with about one thousand men in all. Phillips says the force he took farthest south was 450 mounted men and one howitzer. His February 14 report, relayed by Thayer, says the attack was made by his advance under Willetts and the enemy were Seminoles, Choctaws and Texans; his February 16 report says Jumper's Chickasaw and Seminole regiment was broken to pieces in the late battle.
claims.rationale: Expedition and column strengths, not a count of the advance engaged; no Confederate figure inspected. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Phillips's relayed report says the attack was made by his advance under Major Willetts. His February 15 letter to John Jumper refers to Jumper's personal bravery and his defeat in the late engagement. Britton credits the rout to Phillips. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant Colonel John Jumper and Major Charles Willette; the live page gives the same.
claims.rationale: Command roles from interested reports and a history; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit. The reports spell the Union major 'Willetts'.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. Phillips's relayed report says the enemy were completely routed; the itinerary says they were routed and pursued a considerable distance; Britton says the action lasted less than half an hour. The frozen description says the poorly armed Confederates made a determined stand for half an hour, and that fear of fresh Confederate forces led the Federals to retire to Fort Gibson.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The return to Fort Gibson is the expedition's end, not the engagement's result.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads Unknown, while the frozen description says 47 Confederates were killed; the live field reads 47 (US 0; CS 47). Phillips's February 14 report, relayed by Thayer, gives 47 killed with wounded unknown; the itinerary and Britton give 49 Confederate dead left on the field. Phillips's February 24 report gives about 250 killed and 4 wounded for the whole expedition.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The expedition total is not assigned to this record; no Union loss for February 13 is given.

open_questions: Willette's own report (if any), Wright's report (No. 3, read at its opening), Inclosures Nos. 1-2 (read and not selected) and any Confederate report of Jumper or Maxey on Middle Boggy remain deferred. The live page's empty description gives no independent account.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam's, 1899) is a retrospective history described on its title page as based upon official reports and the author's observations; it relays figures from Union and Confederate reports, so it is not independent of the Official Records families, and is treated as partly a participant's interested Union account. Phillips's February 1864 reports, with Thayer's relay of his February 14 report and the brigade itinerary printed with them, are one family of interested Union accounts. No Confederate report on Middle Boggy was located in the inspected pages. Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIV, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
